title: Freshwater catfish

names.note: Dictionary: 'freshwater catfish (nyungkul) (yalanji - julaji) Sometimes called walarrji, "with whiskers"'.
Dictionary: 'literally "with whiskers". Freshwater catfish are sometimes called this'. Built on walarr 'whiskers, beard'.

scientificName: Eel-tailed catfishes (Plotosidae: Neosilurus, Tandanus and relatives) and fork-tailed catfishes (Ariidae: Neoarius and relatives)

identification.basis: The dictionary defines julaji, kanyaji and walarrji as 'freshwater catfish', which names the group, not a species. The species differ by river: the Bloomfield and Daintree streams of the dictionary's speakers hold the Wet Tropics tandan (Tandanus tropicanus), while the upper Mitchell holds Hyrtl's catfish (Neosilurus hyrtlii), the black catfish (N. ater) and fork-tailed catfishes. Which of these Western Yalanji speakers call julaji or kanyaji is not recorded.

summary: Freshwater catfish are **[julaji](word:julaji)** in the Yalanji dialect and **[kanyaji](word:kanyaji)** in Nyungkul, and are sometimes called **[walarrji](word:walarrji)**, 'with whiskers' [ref:hershberger1982]. They are whiskered, scaleless fish of creeks, rivers and waterholes, and **all of them carry sharp, venomous fin spines** [ref:foa-hyrtl]. They were caught on [lines](entry:hooks-and-lines), in [nets](entry:nets) and in poisoned waterholes, and on the Palmer River a catfish spine made the barb of the fish-hook [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Names
Description
sections.body:
Two families of catfish live in the rivers of Kuku Yalanji country.

**Eel-tailed catfish** (family Plotosidae) are named for their tapering, eel-like tail. **Hyrtl's catfish** (*Neosilurus hyrtlii*) is dark brown to light silver-grey, white underneath, with dark brown to yellow fins. It grows to 40 cm but is commonly about 20 cm. It eats insects, very small crustaceans and some detritus [ref:foa-hyrtl].

**Fork-tailed catfish** (family Ariidae) have a forked tail. The **blue catfish** (*Neoarius graeffei*) is dusky grey with a bluish tinge above and pale cream to pinkish below. It reaches 60 cm, commonly 35 cm, and eats almost anything: small fish, prawns, insects, worms, plants and detritus [ref:foa-blue]. The **highfin catfish** (*Neoarius berneyi*) is silvery-bronze to dark grey and grows to about 45 cm [ref:foa-highfin].

The stiff spines at the front of the back fin and the two side (pectoral) fins are **very sharp and venomous** [ref:foa-hyrtl] [ref:foa-blue] [ref:foa-highfin].

sections.heading: What it can be confused with
sections.body:
Three things in a northern river pool get called 'catfish', and one more gets mistaken for one.

- **Eel-tailed catfish** (Hyrtl's and black catfish, *Neosilurus*): the tail tapers to a point and runs into a long, continuous fin along the back and belly. Hyrtl's is pale brown to silver-grey with a small mouth; the black catfish is darker and heavier [ref:foa-hyrtl] [ref:angfa-ater].
- **Fork-tailed catfish** (blue and highfin catfish, *Neoarius*): a plainly forked tail, a bony shield on the head, and the males carry the eggs in their mouths [ref:foa-blue] [ref:foa-highfin].
- **Both** have whiskers and the sharp venomous spines at the front of the back fin and the two side fins, which no other fish in the pool has [ref:foa-hyrtl] [ref:foa-blue].
- **[Eels](entry:eels)** look like an eel-tailed catfish at a glance in the torchlight, but they have no spines, no whiskers and a snake's head, and they barely reach the Mitchell at all.
- **[Sleepy cod](entry:sleepy-cod)** is a big-mouthed, mottled fish that sits on the bottom among snags; it has no whiskers and a rounded tail [ref:angfa-sleepy].

If you are not sure, look at the tail and the spines before you put a hand anywhere near it.

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **By day**, Hyrtl's catfish keep close to the bottom in the deep water, around two metres down, so you rarely see them; where the water is open and clear they form dense schools, which is thought to be a defence against predators [ref:pusey2004-hyrtlii] [ref:zootaxa2004-hyrtlii].
- **By night**, they come into the shallows, as little as 30 cm deep, and work the sand with their whiskers [ref:pusey2004-hyrtlii]. A torch along the edge of a sand bank after dark shows them nosing along the bottom, often where the [cherabin](entry:cherabin) are out grazing.
- **Cormorants and darters** fishing a pool are the daytime sign that there are catfish-sized fish in it [ref:wiki-darter].
- **In the first floods**, black catfish run upstream to spawn in half a metre of water among grass and woody debris [ref:angfa-ater].
- **A dropped spine** in the sand at a camp is the sign someone has already been cleaning catfish there; handle the head with a stick.

sections.heading: Where it lives
sections.body: Catfish live in creeks, rivers and waterholes. Hyrtl's catfish lives in still or flowing water, in streams, billabongs and pools [ref:foa-hyrtl], and the blue catfish lives in clear or muddy, fast or slow fresh water and in estuaries [ref:foa-blue].

sections.heading: Who eats whom, and when
sections.body:
The catfish is the night shift of the [waterhole](entry:waterhole). Hyrtl's catfish spends the day near the floor of the deep water and forages at night in the shallows, where its small mouth takes small things: snails and freshwater mussels, crustaceans, mayfly nymphs, caddis and midge larvae, and detritus [ref:pusey2004-hyrtlii]. The black catfish takes molluscs, insects and prawns [ref:angfa-ater]. In the Mitchell River diet studies, prawns featured prominently in Hyrtl's catfish, along with the other big-bodied or big-mouthed fish of the pool [ref:jardine2012].

**Catfish, bream and prawns together.** The three share one pool but split it by time and place. The [black bream](entry:black-bream) feeds by day around the rocks, logs and fast shallow runs, and takes prawns there [ref:angfa-grunter] [ref:crook2021] [ref:davis2010]. The catfish takes them at night on the sand shallows, which is exactly when and where the prawns come out to graze the algae [ref:pusey2004-hyrtlii] [ref:lammers2009] [ref:cdu2016]. So the [cherabin](entry:cherabin) is hunted around the clock, by day over rock and by night over sand, which is one reason the prawns that survive to the late dry are the big males under the rock bars [ref:cdu2016].

**What eats the catfish.** Its spines are its defence, and they work: most predators take small fish. Even so, [freshwater crocodiles](entry:freshwater-crocodile) eat more fish as they grow [ref:tucker1996]; a big [barramundi](entry:barramundi)'s diet is about 60 per cent fish [ref:ntgov-barra]; darters spear fish underwater and little black cormorants hunt them in flocks [ref:wiki-darter] [ref:wiki-little-black-cormorant]; and whistling kites and the sea-eagle take fish and carrion from the surface and the banks [ref:wiki-whistling-kite]. Dead catfish in a shrinking pool are crocodile and kite food.

**Through the year.** Black catfish spawn on upstream migrations at peak flood, usually November to December, and drift back downstream when it is done [ref:angfa-ater]. The fork-tailed catfish spawn from the late dry into the wet and the males mouth-brood the eggs for weeks [ref:foa-blue] [ref:foa-highfin]. In the late dry the pools contract and fish biomass falls, from short food and from predation, so the catfish you find in October are the survivors of a crowded pool [ref:asfb2018-flinders].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body:
Fish could be taken at any time of year [ref:anderson1996]. Two seasonal moments stand out in the sources.

- **Late dry season.** As the smaller creeks dry back into separate waterholes, fish are trapped in them. This was when Bloomfield people used [plant poisons](entry:fish-poisoning) [ref:anderson1996], and when Roth saw poisons put into drying holes elsewhere [ref:roth1901].
- **Spawning.** The highfin catfish usually spawns in the late dry, September to October, sometimes into February [ref:foa-highfin]; the blue catfish spawns from the late dry to the end of the wet. In both, the **male carries the eggs and young in his mouth**, for 4–6 weeks in the blue catfish [ref:foa-blue] [ref:foa-highfin]. Hyrtl's catfish breeds at about 12 months old [ref:foa-hyrtl].

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
Catfish is good eating, and freshwater fish of all kinds were a regular food on the inland creeks.

The spine itself was useful. On the Palmer River, the Mitchell's big northern tributary, the Kuku Mini (Roth's 'Koko-minni') made fish-hooks with a wooden shank and a bone barb, the barb being 'either from kangaroo-bone, or from one of the spines of the "cat-fish"' [ref:roth1901].

The fishing words in the dictionary include **[badur](word:badur)** 'hook and line', **[mandurr](word:mandurr)** 'bait (any kind)' and **[kuyu](word:kuyu)** 'fish' [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: How it was caught and cooked
sections.body:
**The Palmer River hook (Kuku Mini).** A wooden shank with a barb of kangaroo bone or catfish spine lashed on at a sharp angle. Further north, around Princess Charlotte Bay, Roth saw the barb fixed with kangaroo-tail tendon and grevillea gum [ref:roth1901].

**[Poisoning](entry:fish-poisoning) a drying waterhole (middle Palmer River).** Roth recorded these poisons on the middle Palmer [ref:roth1901]:

1. Throw the bark of *Adenanthera abrosperma* into the water; or
2. Throw in leaves of the red stringybark (*Eucalyptus resinifera*) and leave them one to three days, depending on the size of the pool. An ironbark was used the same way and worked faster.

E. Palmer told Roth that *Barringtonia racemosa* was also used on the Mitchell, Laura and Lynd rivers [ref:roth1901].

**Muddying.** In a small shallow pool, stir up the mud with your feet, then hit or [spear](entry:spear-and-woomera) the fish as they come up. Roth called this 'a common procedure everywhere' [ref:roth1901].

**[Nets](entry:nets) on the inland rivers.** The Koko-yellanji of the Laura used an oval-framed net they called *jikan-ikan* (Roth's spelling). On the Palmer the same kind of net was strung with *Acacia leptocarpa* twine on a large frame and worked by two people [ref:roth1901].

**Cooking.** Roast the fish straight on the coals, **[dindal](word:dindal)** 'to roast on coals' [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
**The spines.** Catfish spines are venomous and 'may inflict a very painful injury' [ref:foa-hyrtl]. Most stings happen to people taking the fish off the line [ref:isbister2007]. If you are spiked [ref:isbister2007]:

1. Wash the wound.
2. Put the hurt hand or foot in **hot water, about 45°C**, for up to 90 minutes. Test the heat with your other hand first so you don't scald yourself.
3. Get medical care to clean out the wound and check for broken-off spine, and watch for infection over the next days.

**Crocodiles.** Follow the Crocwise rules at any river: stand back from the edge, don't wade in after a snagged line, never clean fish at the water's edge, and take extra care at night, dusk and dawn [ref:crocwise]. See the [freshwater-crocodile](entry:freshwater-crocodile) and [saltwater-crocodile](entry:saltwater-crocodile) entries for which crocodiles live where.

**[Fish poisons](entry:fish-poisoning)** stun and can blind; they are described here as history, not as a method to use [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body:
**Recreational rules (Queensland fresh waters).** Eel-tailed catfish (*Tandanus tandanus*) must be at least 35 cm. The other freshwater catfishes (*Anodontiglanis*, *Neosilurus*, *Neosiluroides*) have no size limit. You may keep **5 freshwater catfish in total**. Fork-tailed catfishes are not listed there; the page sets a general limit of 20 for unlisted freshwater species [ref:qld-limits]. In fresh waters you may use up to six handheld lines with one hook each and must stay within 50 m of them. [Spears](entry:spear-and-woomera), set lines, cast [nets](entry:nets) and crab pots are not allowed [ref:qld-gear].

Native title holders' rights differ from place to place: see each place above, and ask the Traditional Owners before hunting, fishing or gathering.

locations.summary: Catfish live in the Hann's water. On the upper Hann the Court recorded a Possum man's evidence of 'fishing for barra, jewfish, catties and spotties' [ref:fca-possum]; 'jewfish' is the northern anglers' name for the eel-tailed catfish (*Tandanus*) [ref:russell1993]. Downstream in Rinyirru (Lakefield), fork-tailed catfish were caught by nearly half of all fishing parties [ref:russell1993].

sections.heading: Which catfish live here
sections.body: **The records are few.** The Atlas of Living Australia holds 7 catfish records in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru: Hyrtl's catfish (4 records, 1972–2015), Rendahl's catfish (2 records, 1972) and the blue catfish (1 record, 2025) [ref:ala-hann-catfish]. In a survey of Lakefield anglers in 1986–91, 'jewfish (Tandanus spp.)' were caught in fresh water, and 'Fork-tailed catfish (Arius spp.) were caught in both freshwater and estuarine habitats by nearly 45% of the parties surveyed' [ref:russell1993]. Expect both kinds, eel-tailed and fork-tailed, in the deep holes of the Hann.

sections.heading: Its year here
sections.body: **The Hann never stops.** It is fed by springs in the sandstone, and its gauge at Sandy Creek has not recorded a single day without flow since 1968 [ref:bom-105001b] [ref:wetlandinfo-normanby]. In the wet (December to March) the rivers flood out over the plains [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture], and the catfish spread with the water. By September–November the Hann is a low, clear run between deep holes [ref:bom-105001b]. Downstream on the North Kennedy, Catfish Waterhole is one of the deep permanent holes where, 'during the dry season, as water becomes scarce elsewhere, large numbers of wildlife congregate' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. The late-dry holes are where the catfish, the crocodiles and the fishing all meet.

sections.heading: How people fished here
sections.body:
**Possum (upper Hann).** The Court recorded a Possum man's evidence of 'fishing for barra, jewfish, catties and spotties' [ref:fca-possum].

**Thaypan (middle and lower Hann).** 'We get wallaby, barramundi, freshwater fish and turtles and mussels' [ref:fca-thaypan]. Kuku Thaypan Elders recorded 'Rungol (hollow logs) that were cut from the Ku akulumbah Messmate woodland and used as fish traps' [ref:standley2019].

**Kuku Warra (Laura).** A Kuku Warra man described the law of fishing: 'before I pull my line out if I'm fishing I'll sing out to the old people', and 'we must always leave three or four fish on the banks' [ref:fca-kukuwarra].

**Roth, about 1900.** On the North Kennedy and the lower Normanby, Roth passed waterholes with hollow logs lying on their banks, the sign that they had been fished by sinking the logs and lifting them out with the fish inside [ref:roth1901]. On the Palmer River a catfish spine made the barb of the fish-hook (see above) [ref:roth1901]. No published record names a catfish method for the Hann itself.

sections.heading: Safety here
sections.body: Both crocodiles live in this river system. In Rinyirru the rangers' rules are to 'always stand a few metres back from the water's edge' and 'never clean fish or discard fish scraps near the water's edge' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-safe]. Mind the spines when you take a catfish off the line.

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The upper Hann is the Possum People's country and the middle and lower Hann are Thaypan country, both recognised by the Federal Court in November 2023 [ref:fca-possum] [ref:fca-thaypan]. In Rinyirru, Traditional Owners 'use the park to camp, fish and hunt' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-2013]. Everyone else needs the Traditional Owners' permission to be on their country.

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: In Kuku Thaypan (Awu Alaya), the language of the Thaypan people of the middle and lower Hann, catfish is **arrmbil** [ref:hgdb].

locations.summary: On the upper Mitchell around [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) the common catfish are eel-tailed catfish (*Neosilurus*), with fork-tailed catfish in the bigger holes [ref:ala-catfish].

sections.heading: Where they live here
sections.body: [Karma Waters Station](place:karma-waters) sits on the north side of the Mitchell River, about 25 km west of Mount Carbine [ref:karmawaters]. The Atlas of Living Australia holds catfish records right on this stretch: the black catfish (*Neosilurus ater*), recorded by Queensland WildNet in 2008, and Hyrtl's catfish and the highfin catfish, collected for the Queensland Museum. Across the whole Mitchell drainage the Atlas holds more than 100 eel-tailed catfish records (mostly Hyrtl's and black catfish, with Dahl's and Rendahl's catfish) and more than 60 fork-tailed catfish records [ref:ala-catfish].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body:
**Native title.** In 2013 the Federal Court recognised Western Yalanji native title that includes rights to hunt, fish and gather, and to take and use the water, held through the Western Yalanji Aboriginal Corporation RNTBC [ref:fca2013]. A further 170,827 ha was recognised in August 2026; Elder Rose Snider said it meant going back to Country to teach the kids 'how to hunt and fish' [ref:nit2026wy]. Under section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993*, native title holders do not need a licence or permit to fish for personal, domestic or non-commercial communal needs [ref:alrc].

[Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) is a working station [ref:karmawaters]. Visitors need the station's permission, and the Western Yalanji Traditional Owners' permission, to fish its holes.

**At Karma Waters.** Karma Waters Station falls under the earlier 1998 *Western Yalanji or 'Sunset' Peoples v Pedersen* consent determination, the first consent determination of native title over a pastoral property in Australia [ref:wyac2020] [ref:kw-about]. See the [Karma Waters guide](/dictionaries/kuku_yalanji/country/places/karma-waters) for what it covers, and ask the Traditional Owners and the station before hunting, fishing or gathering.

locations.summary: On Eastern Kuku Yalanji country, Bloomfield people caught catfish on [lines](entry:hooks-and-lines) of bark [twine](entry:string-and-twine) with [lawyer-cane](entry:lawyer-cane) thorn hooks, baited with [grubs](entry:witchetty-grub), [small prawns](entry:cherabin) or [frogs](entry:frogs) [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Where they live here
sections.body: In the Daintree drainage, which includes the Bloomfield, the common catfish is a different one, the Wet Tropics tandan (*Tandanus tropicanus*), with a few black catfish records [ref:ala-catfish]. Bloomfield people fished for catfish 'in freshwater creeks and waterholes' [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Uses here
sections.body: On the inland creeks Bloomfield people fished with [lines](entry:hooks-and-lines) for '[turtle](entry:freshwater-turtle), [eelfish](entry:eels), catfish and perch' [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: How they were caught and cooked here
sections.body:
**[Hook and line](entry:hooks-and-lines) in a creek or waterhole (Bloomfield Kuku Yalanji)** [ref:anderson1996]:

1. Make the line from the bark of *Sterculia quadrifolia*, twisted into [twine](entry:string-and-twine).
2. Make the hook from a thorn of the [lawyer cane](entry:lawyer-cane) (*Calamus australis*).
3. Bait it with a grub, a [small freshwater prawn](entry:cherabin) or a small [frog](entry:frogs).
4. Hold the line in your hand, or tie it to a stick set into the bank.
5. Line fishing was mostly women's work, though men did it too.

**[Poisoning](entry:fish-poisoning) a drying waterhole.** At Bloomfield in the late dry, people used the bark and leaves of [*Erythrophleum chlorostachys*](entry:ironwood), smashed together under water, or the stems of [*Barringtonia racemosa*](entry:fish-poison-plants). The stunned fish floated up and were collected. Divers had to keep their eyes shut tight, and the hole could not be used again until a storm and flood refreshed it [ref:anderson1996].

**Cooking.** Bigger catches, such as [eels](entry:eels), [turtles](entry:freshwater-turtle) and [cassowaries](entry:cassowary), were cut up and baked in the [earth oven](entry:earth-oven), **[kurrma](word:kurrma)**, which Bloomfield people made like this [ref:anderson1996]:

1. Heat round [stones](entry:stone) that are known not to crack in a fire, and dig a hole nearby.
2. Lift the hot stones into the hole with lawyer-cane tongs.
3. Put the food, with eucalyptus, acacia or [wild-ginger](entry:wild-ginger) leaves for flavour, into a [bark trough](entry:bark-troughs) on the stones.
4. Pack more hot stones around and on top, cover with [tea-tree bark](entry:paperbark) and then sand or earth, and leave it to cook for several hours.
